note: Unserved historical source before the approved E3 positional re-sequence. These 42 older foundation seeds were replaced; old ids here identify the pre-E3 source, not the current bank. They retain historical errors and make no current teaching/review claim. Advanced displaced seeds are preserved separately for E4.

seed.q: A feature looks values up by key thousands of times per request and never needs them in order. Why does the choice of data structure matter here?
opts: Each structure makes a different set of operations cheap, and lookup by key is cheap only in some of them
Every structure supports the same operations, so only total memory changes
The structure affects how the code reads, but the operation costs are the same
The structure fixes the order values come back in, which this feature depends on
seed.e: Picking a structure is picking which operations are cheap: a hash map answers lookup by key in average O(1), while an unsorted array has to scan and costs O(n). The idea that structures differ only in memory or in readability is the misconception here - the cost of the operation you perform most is what actually changes, and this feature explicitly does not need ordering.
seed.intro: The feature names one operation it performs constantly. Ask what differs between structures for that one operation.

seed.q: If algorithm A does fewer operations than algorithm B for every input size, A is generally:
seed.e: Doing fewer operations for the same work means A is more efficient than B.

seed.q: An algorithm whose running time does not change as the input grows is said to run in:
seed.e: Constant time, written O(1), means the number of steps is bounded by a fixed amount however large n is - reading a[i] is the standard example, since it costs the same at n = 10 and at n = 10 million. Linear time would rise in step with n, and quadratic and exponential rise faster still; all three change when the input changes, which the stem rules out.
seed.intro: Compare the step count at n = 10 with the step count at n = 10 million before naming the class.

seed.q: Which Big-O describes linear time?
seed.e: O(n) means the running time grows in direct proportion to the input size n.

seed.q: For n = 1,000,000, which of these growth rates means the most work?
seed.e: At n = 1,000,000 the four come to roughly 20, 1e6, 2e7 and 1e12 steps, so n² is about fifty thousand times more work than n log n and a million times more than n. The order O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) holds for every large n, which is why an accidental nested loop over a big collection is the classic performance bug.
seed.intro: Substitute the million for n and compare four numbers rather than four shapes.

seed.q: What is the time complexity of accessing an array element by its index?
seed.e: For an array held in one contiguous block, a[i] is a single address computation - base + i × element size - so the cost does not depend on the length. This is access by index only: finding a value whose index you do not know still costs O(n). JavaScript gives you this while the engine keeps the array packed; assigning far past the end makes V8 switch the array to a dictionary representation, which is one reason to avoid holes.
seed.intro: Index access computes an address instead of looking for anything. Ask whether that computation depends on how many elements exist.

seed.q: An array `a` holds 5 elements. Which expression reads the last one?
seed.e: With zero-based indexing a 5-element array has valid indexes 0 through 4, so the last element is a[a.length - 1], here a[4]. Both a[5] and a[a.length] read one past the end and evaluate to undefined rather than throwing, and a[-1] is only a property named "-1" that was never set - JavaScript has no negative indexing, though a.at(-1) does count back from the end.
seed.intro: List the valid indexes for five elements, then check what each expression actually evaluates to.

seed.q: Why is inserting an element at the beginning of an array O(n)?
opts: Arrays must be re-sorted after every insertion
Every element after the insertion point moves one slot to the right
Inserting always allocates a brand-new backing buffer
The array's length has to be recomputed by counting elements
seed.e: Contiguous storage puts index i at a fixed offset, so making room at the front moves all n existing elements one slot right: unshift on a 40-element array touched all 40 indexes, while push touched one. Reallocation can also happen when the buffer is full, but it is not the reason the cost is linear - the shifting happens even when there is spare capacity.
seed.intro: The new element needs slot 0, which is already occupied. Ask what has to happen to everything after it.

seed.q: Compared with linked lists, what is a key property of arrays?
opts: They store elements in one contiguous block of memory
They store a next-pointer alongside every element
They can grow in place without ever copying elements
They keep elements sorted as they are inserted
seed.e: Contiguity is what buys O(1) index access: the address is base + i × element size, with no traversal. A linked list instead stores a pointer per node, which is what lets it splice in the middle without shifting but costs O(n) to reach position k. In JavaScript this is an engine choice rather than a guarantee - V8 keeps a dense array packed but moves a sparse one to a dictionary representation, and delete on an element leaves a hole while length stays the same.
seed.intro: One structure computes where element i lives; the other has to follow links to reach it.

seed.q: Which approach checks whether a normalized string is a palindrome in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
opts: Sort the characters and compare adjacent values
Compare characters from both ends while moving two indexes inward
Insert every character into a set and check its size
Generate every permutation and look for the reverse
seed.e: A palindrome reads the same in both directions, so comparing mirrored positions with two indexes settles it in at most n/2 comparisons and keeps only those two indexes - O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Sorting the characters destroys the positions the property is about, a set of characters costs O(n) extra space and answers a different question, and generating permutations is factorial work for a linear problem.
seed.intro: Work out the time and the extra space each approach needs before comparing them with the two budgets.

seed.q:
What does the method chain return?

```js
["ab", "cd"].join("").split("").reverse().join("");
```
seed.e: join("") turns ["ab","cd"] into "abcd", split("") gives ["a","b","c","d"], reverse mutates that array to ["d","c","b","a"], and the final join("") makes "dcba" - the array-valued option is what you would get if the last join were missing. The idiom is not safe for arbitrary text: split("") cuts on UTF-16 code units, so reversing "ab😀" produces a broken surrogate pair, where [...s].reverse().join("") keeps the emoji intact.
seed.intro: Note the type after each call: one of these steps hands you an array rather than a string.

seed.q: What is the average-case time to look up a value by key in a hash table?
seed.e: Hashing the key produces a bucket index, so the lookup goes to one bucket instead of scanning: with 100 keys spread over 64 buckets the deepest bucket held 5 entries, a small constant rather than a function of n. This is the average case, and it assumes a hash that distributes keys and a load factor kept bounded by resizing - with every key in one bucket the same lookup walks all n entries and becomes O(n).
seed.intro: The key is turned into a bucket index directly. Ask what has to be true for that bucket to hold only a few entries.

seed.q: In the worst case (many collisions), a hash table lookup can degrade to:
seed.e: If the hash sends every key to the same bucket the lookup walks that whole chain: with 400 colliding keys, finding the last one took 400 probes, against 3 when the same 400 keys were spread across 512 buckets. That is O(n), no better than scanning an array, and it is why a hash function an attacker can predict turns into a denial-of-service vector. O(log n) would require an ordered structure, which a hash table does not maintain.
seed.intro: Picture every key landing in one bucket. What is left to search?

seed.q: In JavaScript, a Map or plain object is most often used to provide:
opts: Ordered range queries between two keys
Automatic balancing of a search tree
A fixed memory footprint regardless of size
seed.e: Both give average O(1) access by key, which is the reason to reach for either. They are not interchangeable: a plain object coerces keys to strings, so o[1] and o["1"] are one entry, and it iterates integer-like keys in ascending numeric order before the rest, while a Map accepts any value as a key (a Map holding 1 and "1" has size 2) and iterates in insertion order. Neither answers range queries, neither maintains a tree, and both grow with the number of entries.
seed.intro: Think about why you would reach for a Map instead of an array of key-value pairs.

seed.q: What property must a value have to work as a hash table key?
opts: It must be kept in sorted order
It must map to a consistent hash value
It must be unique across all programs
seed.e: Insertion hashes the key to choose a bucket and every lookup hashes it again; if the two hashes differ, the lookup searches the wrong bucket and the entry is invisible - which is exactly what happens when an object is mutated after being used as a key in a table hashed by its contents. Keys need not be integers (a JavaScript Map takes any value, and even NaN works, because Map compares with SameValueZero), need no global uniqueness, and are never kept sorted.
seed.intro: Follow one key through an insert and then a lookup, and ask what would make the lookup miss.

seed.q: A hash table (hash set) is an excellent choice when you need to:
seed.e: A hash set hashes the value and checks one bucket, so membership does not get slower as the collection grows: scanning a 1000-element array for an absent value took 1000 comparisons, while Set.prototype.has checks a single bucket. What you give up is exactly what the other options ask for - a set has no order, so it cannot be kept sorted or indexed by position, and the bucket array plus per-entry overhead means it is not the minimal-memory choice.
seed.intro: For each option, ask whether hashing the value alone could answer it.

seed.q: What is the amortized time complexity of push and pop on a stack?
seed.e: Push and pop act on the top only, so their cost does not depend on how deep the stack is - pushing onto an array touched one index whether it held 10, 20 or 40 elements, and popping touched one. For an array-backed stack this is amortized O(1): an occasional resize copies all n elements, but doubling the capacity spreads that cost over the pushes that follow. A linked-node stack is O(1) in the worst case as well, because it never resizes.
seed.intro: Only one end is touched. Ask whether anything else in the structure has to move.

seed.q: Which everyday feature is commonly implemented with a stack?
seed.e: Undo uses a stack: the last action performed is the first one undone (LIFO).

seed.q: Which graph traversal uses a queue to visit nodes level by level?
opts: In-order traversal of a binary tree
seed.e: BFS holds its frontier in a FIFO queue: dequeue a node, enqueue its unvisited neighbors, so everything at distance k is processed before anything at distance k+1 - on A to {B,C}, B to {D,E}, C to {F} the visit order is A, B, C, D, E, F. Swap the queue for a stack and the same code becomes depth-first, visiting A, C, F, B, E, D - one branch to the end before the other; in-order traversal and backtracking are likewise stack- or recursion-driven, so they dive deep before going wide.
seed.intro: Ask what each traversal does with a node's neighbors: all of them next, or one of them next?

seed.q: A sliding window needs to add items at one end and drop them from either end as it advances. Which structure supports that in O(1) per operation?
opts: A singly linked list with only a head pointer
seed.e: A deque keeps handles on both head and tail, so adding or removing at either end is O(1) - what a sliding-window maximum or a capacity-limited undo/redo pair needs. A singly linked list with only a head can drop the front cheaply but needs O(n) to reach the tail, a search tree costs O(log n) per operation, and a hash set has no ends at all.
seed.intro: For each option, work out what it costs to reach and remove at the far end.

seed.q: What is the time complexity of accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list by position?
seed.e: Nodes sit wherever they were allocated, so position k is reached only by following k next-pointers from the head: on a 100-node list, index 50 cost 50 hops and index 99 cost 99. That is O(n) in the worst case, against O(1) for an array's address computation. What the list buys in exchange is O(1) insertion after a node you already hold, with no shifting - removing that node is not free in a singly linked list, since its predecessor has to be found by walking from the head.
seed.intro: There is no address arithmetic available here. Ask how you actually get from the head to position k.

seed.q: A doubly linked list differs from a singly linked list because each node also stores:
opts: A reference to the previous node
A reference to the head of the list
Its position index in the list
A copy of the previous node's value
seed.e: Each node keeps prev as well as next, so traversal runs in both directions and a node you already hold can be removed in O(1) - a singly linked list has to walk from the head to find the predecessor first. The cost is one extra pointer per node and two links to keep consistent on every insertion and removal, which is where doubly linked list bugs come from.
seed.intro: Ask which operations a singly linked list cannot do without walking from the head again.

seed.q: Given a reference to the node you want to change, what does a linked list do better than an array?
opts: Random access by index in O(1)
Insertion and deletion without shifting elements
seed.e: Relinking pointers inserts or removes a node in constant time, while an array must move every element after the position: a front insert into a 100,000-element array costs 100,000 moves, the list costs one pointer write. Random access stays the array's advantage, because reaching index 50,000 in the list took 50,000 hops, and each node also carries a pointer, so a list uses more memory per element, not less.
seed.intro: One structure computes an address from an index; the other only relinks pointers. Ask what each has to touch to remove a middle element.

seed.q: Which technique detects a cycle in a linked list using only constant extra space?
opts: Two pointers moving at different speeds
Binary search over the node values
seed.e: Floyd's fast and slow pointers meet inside a cycle and use two variables, so the extra space is O(1). A visited-node set detects the same cycle but stores up to n node references, which the constant-space requirement rules out; binary search and sorting both need an ordering that a list of links does not provide.
seed.intro: The list could hold a million nodes. Work out how much extra memory each approach needs at that size.

seed.q: In a singly linked list you hold a pointer to a node that is not the last one, and no pointer to its predecessor. How do you delete it?
opts: Reverse the list and delete from the front
Copy the next node's value in and skip the next node
Sort the list and drop the duplicate
Set the head to null and rebuild the list
seed.e: Copying the successor's value into this node and unlinking the successor removes one value in O(1): applied to the node holding 2, the list [1,2,3,4] becomes [1,3,4]. It cannot be used on the last node, whose next is null, and it silently invalidates any outside pointer that still refers to the successor node.
seed.intro: You cannot reach the predecessor's link, so change what this node holds instead.

seed.q: Every correct recursion must have a:
opts: Base case that stops the recursion
seed.e: A base case terminates the recursion; without one it would recurse forever.

seed.q: What happens if a recursion has no reachable base case?
opts: It recurses until a stack overflow
seed.e: Each pending call keeps a frame on the call stack, so with no reachable base case the frames never pop: Node 22 throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded after roughly 12,500 frames in a simple function. Nothing optimizes it away either, because V8 does not implement proper tail calls, and a tail-recursive function in strict mode overflows at the same depth.
seed.intro: Every call that has not returned still occupies a frame. Ask what runs out first.

seed.q: A naive recursive Fibonacci (recomputing subproblems) has time complexity of about:
seed.e: Every call fans out into two more and the same subproblems are recomputed, so the call count multiplies by roughly 1.618 per step: measured in Node 22, fib(10) makes 177 calls, fib(20) 21,891, fib(25) 242,785 and fib(30) 2,692,537. That is exponential, bounded above by 2^n (the exact rate is the golden ratio to the n), which is why O(n) or O(n squared) cannot describe it.
seed.intro: Each call spawns two more. Count how the number of calls changes when n grows by one.

seed.q: Memoization speeds up recursion by:
opts: Storing each subproblem's result so it is computed once
Making every individual call cheaper to execute
Replacing the recursion with an equivalent loop
Shrinking the recursion depth to O(log n)
seed.e: Memoization keeps a table of results, so each distinct input is computed once and later requests are lookups: in Node 22 naive fib(35) makes 29,860,703 calls while the memoized version makes 69. Individual calls are no cheaper, and the recursion is still recursion at depth n, so turning it into a loop is a different technique (tabulation), not what memoization does.
seed.intro: The calls themselves do not get faster. Ask what stops happening.

seed.q: A tail-recursive call is one where the recursive call is:
opts: Placed before the base case check
The last operation performed before returning
Multiplied by the result of another call
Made once for each element of a loop
seed.e: In tail position the recursive call is the last thing the function does, so its frame has no pending work and a compiler may reuse it. return n * f(n - 1) is not tail recursive, because the multiplication still waits on the result. ES2015 specifies proper tail calls, but V8 does not implement them: in Node 22 a strict-mode tail-recursive call at depth 1,000,000 still throws RangeError.
seed.intro: Ask what still has to happen after the inner call returns its value.

seed.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort?
seed.e: Each pass compares adjacent pairs and the passes shrink by one, so a reversed input costs n(n-1)/2 comparisons: measured in Node 22, n = 8 took 28, n = 16 took 120 and n = 32 took 496, all exactly n(n-1)/2. O(n) is the best case only, and only for the early-exit variant, which finished an already-sorted 32-element array in 31 comparisons.
seed.intro: Count the comparisons of the inner pass, then how many passes a fully reversed input forces.

seed.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
seed.e: When the pivot is the smallest or largest remaining element, each partition removes only one element and the recursion is n levels deep, so the comparisons reach n(n-1)/2: with a last-element pivot on already-sorted input, Node 22 measured 28 comparisons at n = 8, 120 at n = 16 and 496 at n = 32. Random or median-of-three pivots restore the O(n log n) average, measured at 138 comparisons for n = 32, but the worst case never disappears.
seed.intro: Picture the partition when every element lands on one side. How many partitions does that take?

seed.q: A typical in-place quicksort, compared with merge sort, is:
opts: Not stable, because partitioning swaps distant elements
Stable whenever the input is already sorted
Stable whenever the pivot is the median
seed.e: Partitioning exchanges elements across the array, so two equal values can end up in the opposite order from the input; that is why standard in-place quicksort is not stable. Merge sort is stable because the merge step takes from the left run whenever the two fronts compare equal. Neither a sorted input nor a perfect median pivot restores stability, they only change quicksort's running time.
seed.intro: Watch where partitioning sends an element: to the neighboring slot, or anywhere across the array?

seed.q: Quicksort partitions the array around a chosen element called the:
seed.e: Quicksort picks a pivot, moves smaller elements before it and larger ones after it, then sorts the two sides. The choice matters as well as the name: with a last-element pivot on already-sorted input the partitions are maximally lopsided and comparisons hit n(n-1)/2, measured as 496 at n = 32, while a random pivot averaged 138. A root is the top of a tree and a sentinel is a placeholder node, neither of which quicksort uses.
seed.intro: The name comes from what the element does: everything else is placed relative to it.

seed.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
seed.e: Every comparison halves the remaining range, so the number of steps is how often n can be halved: measured in Node 22, the range shrinks to nothing in 10 steps for n = 1,000, 20 steps for n = 1,000,000 and 30 for n = 1,000,000,000. Multiplying n by 1,000 adds ten comparisons, which is what log n means; O(n log n) would be the cost of sorting the array, not of searching it.
seed.intro: Ask how many times you can halve a range of n before only one element is left.

seed.q: Linear search on an unsorted list is, in the worst case:
seed.e: A scan stops only when it finds the target or runs out of elements, so the worst case is a missing value or one in the last position: n comparisons, measured as 100,000 for a 100,000-element array. Finding it in the first slot is the best case at a single comparison, while a random position averages about n/2, which is still O(n) because a constant factor does not change the growth. O(log n) would require sorted input, which the stem rules out.
seed.intro: Think about where the value has to be for the scan to do the most work.

seed.q: For about 1,000,000 sorted elements, binary search needs roughly how many comparisons in the worst case?
seed.e: Halving a million takes about 20 steps because 2 to the 20th is 1,048,576, and running the search over a sorted array of 1,000,000 in Node 22 never exceeded 20 comparisons. The useful form of this is that every doubling of n costs one extra comparison, so a billion elements need only about 30. The 500,000 answer is what halving the work once, rather than halving repeatedly, would give.
seed.intro: Start at a million and keep halving. Count how many halvings reach one.

seed.q: Compared with linear search, binary search trades extra requirements for:
opts: A constant number of comparisons regardless of size
Far fewer comparisons on large sorted inputs
seed.e: Binary search examines about log2 n elements instead of up to n: for 100,000 elements a scan made 100,000 comparisons while the binary search made 14. It is not constant time, since the count still grows with n, and it uses no extra memory, so the price is the sorted input rather than space.
seed.intro: Both searches answer the same question. Compare only how many elements each one has to look at.

seed.q: A binary tree of n nodes that is balanced has a height of about:
seed.e: Level k holds up to 2 to the k nodes, so n nodes fit in about log2 n levels: measured, a perfectly balanced tree of 1,023 nodes has height 9 and one of 1,048,575 nodes has height 19. O(n) is not a nonsense answer but the unbalanced case, where each node has one child and the tree degenerates into a list; keeping height at log n is exactly what balancing is for.
seed.intro: Each level can hold twice as many nodes as the one above it. Ask how many levels n nodes need.

seed.q: What is the defining ordering property of a binary search tree (BST)?
opts: All left-subtree values are smaller, all right-subtree values larger
Only the immediate left child is smaller and the right child larger
All left-subtree values are larger, all right-subtree values smaller
No ordering is imposed between a node and its descendants
seed.e: The invariant covers entire subtrees: a node buried deep on the left must still be smaller than the root, which is what lets a search discard a whole subtree at each step. Checking only the immediate children is the classic mistake and accepts trees whose in-order traversal is not sorted. Implementations usually assume distinct keys and send duplicates consistently to one side.
seed.intro: Ask whether the rule constrains the two children only, or everything beneath them.

seed.q: Self-balancing BSTs such as AVL or Red-Black trees exist primarily to:
opts: Bound the height so operations stay O(log n)
Reduce the memory each node needs
Store duplicate keys without extra work
Traverse the tree without using recursion
seed.e: Rotations after each insert and delete keep the height near log2 n, and the height is what bounds the worst case: inserting 1..1023 in sorted order produced an AVL tree only 10 levels deep, while the same inserts left a plain BST as a 1023-node chain. Memory runs the other way, since every node has to carry an extra height or color field. Duplicate keys and recursion are unrelated to balancing - AVL insertion is usually written recursively.
seed.intro: Ask what goes wrong in a plain BST when the keys happen to arrive in sorted order.

seed.q: Deleting a BST node that has two children must keep the ordering property intact. Which value should replace the deleted one?
opts: The value at the tree's root
Its left child, dropping the right subtree
seed.e: The in-order successor is the smallest value in the right subtree, and the predecessor the largest in the left; either is the only value that still stands above everything on the left and below everything on the right, so the ordering survives. Deleting 200 nodes with the successor rule left the tree valid with all 823 remaining values intact. Splicing in the left child alone also leaves a valid BST, which is why it looks safe, but it silently discards the right subtree: the same 200 deletions left only 364 of the 823 values.
seed.intro: Only one value can sit between the deleted node's two subtrees without breaking the order. Which one is it?
